text: IPv4 addresses are 32 bits, which caps the entire address space at about 4.3 billion unique addresses — nowhere near enough for a planet with billions of phones, laptops, servers, and IoT devices all needing one. The internet has been managing that scarcity for years, mainly through NAT.

IPv6 addresses are 128 bits — not twice as many as IPv4, but roughly 340 undecillion of them. That's large enough that address exhaustion isn't a realistic concern on any human timescale, which removes the need for NAT as a scarcity workaround.

An IPv6 address is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. Two shorthand rules make them easier to write: leading zeros in each group can be dropped, and one single run of consecutive all-zero groups can be collapsed to a double colon — but only once per address. Applying both rules, 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 shortens down to 2001:db8:85a3::8a2e:370:7334.

Almost no organization has fully retired IPv4 — the realistic migration path is dual-stack, where a device and network run IPv4 and IPv6 at the same time, using whichever protocol the destination actually supports. Azure and AWS both support dual-stack networking for exactly this reason.
